Today's drop in gold prices was highly unusual.

Gold prices fell -3.4% today, marking one of the rarest single-day declines of the last two decades.

Since 2006, gold has recorded an average daily change of +0.05%, with a standard deviation of 1.19%.

Today’s selloff registered a Z-score of -2.90, placing it deep in the left tail of the distribution.

Statistically, a daily decline this extreme occurs just ~0.2% of the time, or roughly once every 2 years assuming a normal distribution.

Credit card stress is hitting young Americans hardest:

Transitions into serious credit card delinquencies for Americans aged 18-29 rose +0.4 percentage points in Q2 2026, to 10.1%, their highest since Q1 2025.

This marks the 2nd consecutive increase, bringing the rate closer to its highest level since Q4 2010.

Serious delinquencies among this age group have more than doubled since Q2 2021.

Furthermore, transitions into 90+ days delinquent credit card debt among Americans aged 70+ rose +0.3 percentage points in Q2, to 6.3%, their highest since Q3 2011.

At the same time, serious delinquencies among those aged 50-59 rose +0.1 percentage points, to 6.4%, their highest level since Q4 2024.

Credit card stress is spreading across multiple generations.

Tech employment in Silicon Valley is falling:

Employment in the Information sector across San Francisco and the northern part of the Silicon Valley has fallen by -3,007 jobs since March, to 102,529, its lowest since October 2019.

Since the August 2022 peak, the sector has shed -28,914 jobs, or -22%, erasing the entire pandemic-era hiring boom.

By comparison, the decline during the 2001 recession was -17,719 jobs, or -26%.

Meanwhile, employment in the Professional, Scientific and Technical Services sector in the same region has fallen -35,500 jobs since June 2022, a -13.2% decline, to 198,800 jobs, its lowest level since March 2019.

For perspective, following the 2000 Dot-Com Bust, the sector lost -28% of its jobs through October 2003.

The post-pandemic IT hiring boom in San Francisco has completely reversed.

The AI revolution is running into a power bottleneck:

US data center IT power demand is projected to surge +755% from 2025 levels, reaching a record 78.57 gigawatts by 2029.

This year alone, demand is expected to jump +95% to 17.96 gigawatts, and then another +97% in 2027.

This comes as US data centers are set to require 97 gigawatts of power in the 2026 to 2028 period.

Meanwhile, only 21 gigawatts are under construction, and 19 gigawatts of grid capacity are available, leaving a potential 57-gigawatt shortfall.

The gap is widening as increasingly powerful AI systems require far more electricity, while power supply is struggling to keep pace.

At the same time, more complex servers built around Nvidia’s Vera Rubin and Rubin Ultra architectures are expected to push IT power demand 5x from 2025 to 2028.

The AI buildout is running into a significant power constraint.

BREAKING: Global equity funds attracted +$44.1 billion in inflows in the week ending September 23rd, their largest weekly inflow since July 8th.

This follows -$22.3 billion in the prior week, the biggest weekly outflow in 9 months.

Demand was driven by US funds, which saw +$37.6 billion in inflows, the largest weekly intake in 3 months.

At the same time, European funds posted +$2.3 billion in inflows, while Asia attracted +$2.2 billion.

Technology funds saw inflows of +$5.3 billion, the largest weekly inflow since July 29th, followed by healthcare and consumer discretionary at +$804 million and +$492 million, respectively.

Investors are aggressively rotating back into US equities.

AI has been adopted faster than any other technology in history.

In ~4 years, AI went from an idea to a product that more than 1.2 billion people have already used.

In the US alone, 1 in 4 adults now interact with AI every day, with worldwide AI spending expected to hit ~$2.6 trillion this year.

But almost all of that AI lives on a screen, as chatbots answer, draft, advise, then hand information directly back to its user.

This still requires a substantial amount of human interaction, effectively bottlenecking efficiency. 

For example, despite AI agents, the average American still spends 41 minutes on hold every month, which adds up to 2.8 billion hours per year nationwide.

The next phase of AI will be linking it to the real-world in a far more efficient way.

Great move for US Treasury and congrats 🎉

US Treasuries are experiencing one of the worst bear markets in history:

The 30Y US Treasury price return index has dropped -60% since 2020, to ~107, matching its lowest level in 2000.

In other words, in just 6 years, the index has erased nearly 20 years of gains.

By comparison, US nominal GDP has grown +63% over the same period.

This comes as the 30Y Treasury yield has surged +478 basis points from its intraday low of 0.71% set in March 2020.

To put this into perspective, its previous largest drawdown over the past 40 years was -35% during the 2008 Financial Crisis.

We are witnessing a historic bond market decline.

AI agents are becoming a major problem for commerce.

AI agents are flooding commerce, but there is no standard way to verify who an agent represents or whether it is authorized to act.

In other words, unsecure software is spending large amounts of money on behalf of humans and institutions, with the AI agent market set exceed $53 billion by 2030.

In June, Stripe reported that 70% of commands used to access data through its API now come from AI agents.

As a result, Visa, Mastercard and American Express all launched agent commerce protocols in the last year.

Furthermore, Shopify has turned on agentic sales channels by default for ~1 million merchants.

Straightforward, secure transactions are becoming harder to identify.
